Checking that the supplied JSON adheres to this specification. The JSON structure needs to include the "section_name" to be considered valid.

The JSON schema defines a "DiscoveryResult" object with "section_name" (string) and "candidates" (array of "CandidatePaper" objects) as required fields. "CandidatePaper" objects must include "title", "year", and "reason" fields. The goal is to provide between 10 and 15 papers. The task involves a literature search focusing on systematic prediction offsets and residual interpretation. The context framing focuses on a simple instructional example with a fixed predictor.

These papers establish the theoretical foundation for examining residuals to identify systematic biases and assess fixed predictor performance. Foundational works like Anscombe & Tukey (1963) and Cox & Snell (1968) formalize the role of residuals in detecting discrepancies and evaluating fixed predictor outputs. Theil (1965) and Anscombe (1973) highlight the importance of residual analysis to go beyond summary statistics and identify systematic offsets, thus enabling the evaluation of the simple instructional example provided.

These works extend the theoretical foundation for bias detection and fixed predictor evaluation by introducing generalized linear models and additive offsets (Nelder & Wedderburn, 1972). Understanding the distinction between in-sample fitting and validation (Efron, 1983) informs adjustments based on empirical sample mean residuals. Further insights from Belsley, Kuh, & Welsch (1980) and Box (1976) emphasize iterative model criticism and diagnostic functions of residual analysis. Additive models and partial residual analysis (Hastie & Tibshirani, 1986; Buja et al., 2019) confirm that systematic additive terms are the key to unlocking the ability to detect systematic offsets.
